<reason>PRO set a clear decision rule in the opening (does a ban leave the woman who actually carries the pregnancy better off than a statute?) and held CON to it throughout. CON's strongest material—payment as soft enforcer via installments/housing, the "cannot quit at month seven" distinction from ordinary work, and the California-still-offshore example—created real pressure, but its central factual load-bearing claim ("bans deter, shrink demand, don't transfer one-for-one") arrived late as bare assertion against PRO's grounded and unrebutted export story (German/French demand moving to Ukraine/Georgia; India/Thailand closures relocating the market). PRO's pressure questions exposed the real fault line: CON's protected woman is the one who never signs, and CON accepts identical medical risks in unpaid regimes. CON's A2 (payment summons the industry) was a reasonable answer, but PRO's honest concession in A2 ("it does not, directly—and neither does the ban") plus the "two women" closing made the comparison cleaner and easier to decide. PRO pays an execution cost for two clipped turns, and left CON's soft-coercion point only partly answered via escrow, which keeps this competitive rather than decisive.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's handling of "one will give" [B1.7]: turning CON's own dilemma into the case for regulation—"that is precisely what a statute decides; in a regulated regime the buyer's expectation gives"—then asking who decides in Ukraine or Georgia. CON's reply (money enforces what paper voids) was its best counterpunch, but it never showed why the unregulated broker market CON's ban sustains does any better on that score.</best_rebuttal>
